note: Passes on profile and fails on the two criteria that decided the call. Successful is a clear match — technical project manager at Blue Origin plus a program manager role in the Air Force Reserve. Good-to-great is close to a perfect match and he uses the ICP's own framing without prompting: 'I'm at a Manny 1.5 because I'm doing a lot of this.' Not-deconditioned is emphatic: 185-190 lb at 5'10.5", a recent sub-seven-minute mile, in the gym most days. Income fails on the test that matters, which is affordability rather than headline earnings — he makes good money and still cannot reach the price, because alimony at 30% of pre-tax income, $3,000 a month child support and two households leave about $2,000 of discretionary income. Neglected_health fails in the opposite direction from most misses in this corpus: health is not the neglected area, it is the area he manages most actively. He quotes his own A1C to a decimal, monitors his blood pressure at home, is under an orthopedic surgeon, and has already lost 25 lb this year. The ICP describes someone who has let health slide while succeeding elsewhere; this is someone doing everything right whose numbers are drifting anyway because of genetics. Two findings worth carrying up. First, the ICP has no clinical criterion, and this prospect carries an explicit surgeon restriction on the exact movement pattern the programme is built on — he is the clearest case yet that the missing criterion is a screening failure and not just a categorisation gap. Second, 'makes good money' is the wrong test where alimony and child support are involved; the criterion measured his salary and the call was decided by his net.
